items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what changed between release 8 and release 9?
choices: The person following it, not the checklist
The wording of the steps on the wiki page
The speed of the production server in use
items.explanation: The page was identical. A rushed person skipped one line, which is the weakness of memory-based processes.

items.prompt: What is a written checklist, as this unit describes it?
choices: A script the machine runs for you each time
A guarantee that every step runs
A suggestion that nothing enforces
items.explanation: A page can be ignored, skimmed or followed out of order. Only a script makes a step unavoidable.

items.prompt: Do eight clean releases prove a manual process is safe?
choices: Yes, eight in a row proves the steps are complete
No, only that nobody has had a bad day yet
Yes, because people learn the steps by heart
items.explanation: Clean runs show the steps work when followed, not that they will always be followed.

items.prompt: Which step did Tomas skip on release 9?
choices: Installing the outside packages
Pulling the newest code
Restarting the service
items.explanation: The new code needed a new package, and without the install step the restart crashed.

items.prompt: What does downtime mean?
choices: Time the team spends writing up the checklist
Time a server takes to boot up after a restart
A period when users cannot use the service
items.explanation: Downtime is measured from the user's side: any stretch where the service does not work for them.

items.prompt: As steps are added to a manual checklist, the chance at least one is missed:
choices: Stays the same whatever the length
Goes up with every step added
Goes down because people practise
items.explanation: Each extra step is another chance to miss one, so the overall chance climbs.

items.prompt: Is the release 9 failure really about one particular command?
choices: No, it is about relying on memory
Yes, that command is uniquely fragile
Yes, packages never install themselves
items.explanation: Any step in any manual process can be the one that gets skipped. The weakness is the reliance on memory.

items.prompt: What can a script do that a wiki page cannot?
choices: Explain why each step matters to a reader
Shorten the list of steps over time
Run every step in order every time
items.explanation: A script executes the same sequence each time, whoever starts it.

items.prompt: A six-step checklist has run cleanly 40 times. On run 41 a newcomer skips step 4 and the release breaks. What best describes the cause?
choices: The 40 clean runs proved the checklist was complete
Nothing enforced step 4, so memory was the control
The checklist was missing a seventh step all along
Newcomers cannot be trusted to follow any process
items.explanation: Forty clean runs never enforced anything. They only show that the steps work when someone follows them, and on run 41 nobody did.
items.reference:
Same steps, different person
📋 checklist: pull, install, restart
✅ releases 1 to 8: nobody skipped a line
⚡ release 9: one line skipped, crash
📈 more steps means more chances to miss one
Why: a checklist depends on memory, and memory fails on ordinary days, so clean runs prove luck rather than safety.
items.learnMore:
Why manual deploys fail eventually

A written checklist is a suggestion: nothing stops a step being skipped, reordered or run twice. Even a small per-step miss rate compounds, because the chance that every step goes right is multiplied once per step.

Common mistake

Blaming the person. The same checklist in a rushed or tired moment produces the same miss, so the fix is a process that does not rely on memory.
items.reflection: Think of a routine you do from memory, such as locking up or packing a bag. When did you last skip a step, and what would have caught it?

items.prompt: Which change addresses the root cause of release 9?
choices: Run the steps from a script that cannot skip one
Print the checklist on paper and pin it above the desk
Ask Tomas to be much more careful from now on
Add a bold line saying never to skip a step
items.explanation: Reminders and warnings still depend on a person remembering. A script removes that dependence.

items.prompt: At an assumed 2% miss rate per step, which comparison is right?
choices: Both have the same chance because 2% is per step
A 5-step checklist is riskier since each step is rushed
A 10-step checklist has exactly double the 5-step chance
10 steps gives about 18.3%, against 9.6% for 5
items.explanation: The chance of at least one miss is 1 minus 0.98 to the power of the step count: about 9.6% for 5 steps and 18.3% for 10. It is more than the 5-step figure and not simply double.

choices: Agree, since a year of success proves the checklist is complete
Agree, as long as the same person always runs it
A year without a miss shows luck, not enforcement
Disagree, because checklists always fail in year two

items.prompt: What is a deployment?
choices: Writing and reviewing the code for a new feature
Making a built version the one users reach
Running the code on a developer's own laptop
items.explanation: A deployment is the step from a built artifact to running service.

items.prompt: What does repeatability mean?
choices: The same steps, run the same way by anyone
The steps can be rewritten each time to suit the day
Only one named person may ever run them
items.explanation: Repeatability removes dependence on who is running the deploy and what kind of day they are having.

items.prompt: What does idempotency mean?
choices: Running the steps once and never running them again
Running the steps faster on every new attempt
Re-running the steps still ends in a good state
items.explanation: Idempotent steps can be replayed after a failure without compounding errors.

items.prompt: Which is an everyday example of idempotency?
choices: Pressing a doorbell twice and hearing it ring twice
Pressing save twice and still having one profile
Adding an item to a cart twice and getting two
items.explanation: Saving twice leaves the same end state as saving once. The doorbell and the cart both change with every press.

items.prompt: What is an atomic switch?
choices: Moving users to the new version in one step
Updating the files one at a time until done
Restarting every server in turn
items.explanation: Atomic means there is no visible state between old and new.

items.prompt: What is a rollback?
choices: Deleting the new version from the server forever
Rewriting the history of the code
Going back to the last known-good version
items.explanation: A rollback restores the version that was working.

items.prompt: Which term describes swapping a symlink pointer?
choices: Rollback step
Atomic switch
Idempotency
items.explanation: A pointer names either the old folder or the new one, so the swap is one indivisible step.

items.prompt: Which property does a wiki checklist fail to guarantee?
choices: Repeatability
Dependability
Downtime window
items.explanation: A page cannot ensure the same steps run the same way each time.

items.prompt: A deploy fails after step 3 of 5 and is re-run from the start. The second run ends correct, with nothing duplicated. Which property is this?
choices: Atomic switch
Rollback
Repeatability
Idempotency
items.explanation: Re-running after a partial failure and reaching the same good state is idempotency.
items.reference:
Five words, five jobs
🚀 deployment: make the new build the live one
🔁 repeatability: same steps, same way, every time
♻️ idempotency: re-run and still end correct
🔀 atomic switch: users move in one step
↩️ rollback: return to the last good version
Why: each word names one guarantee a careful deploy needs.
items.learnMore:
The deploy vocabulary

Repeatability is about the steps running the same way whoever starts them. Idempotency is about re-running after a partial failure. An atomic switch is about users never seeing a half-way state. Rollback is about returning to a good version after a failed check.

Common mistake

Using the words interchangeably. A pipeline can be repeatable without being idempotent, or switch atomically without any rollback.
items.reflection: Pick any process you rely on at home or work. Which of the five words would it most need, and which could it live without?

items.prompt: Users must never see half the old files and half the new ones. Which property is needed?
choices: Idempotency
Rollback
Atomic switch
Repeatability
items.explanation: Only a single indivisible change of what users reach rules out half-and-half states.

items.prompt: Which step comes first in the pipeline?
choices: Switch the pointer to the new folder
Restart the service for all users
Extract the new release
items.explanation: Preparation starts by unpacking the new version into its own folder.

items.prompt: Which step moves users to the new release?
choices: Extracting the files into a folder
The atomic symlink switch
Installing dependencies for the app
items.explanation: Only the switch changes which release users reach.

items.prompt: Where does the health check sit relative to the switch?
choices: Before it
After it
At the same moment
items.explanation: The check decides whether the switch should happen at all.

items.prompt: While extract and install run, which release serves users?
choices: The new release
Neither, the service is paused
The old release
items.explanation: The old release keeps serving until the switch.

items.prompt: What is a health check?
choices: A person reading through the logs after launch
An automatic test of the candidate version
A written list of steps kept in the wiki
items.explanation: It is a machine-run test of the candidate version.

items.prompt: What is a migration?
choices: A database shape change the new code needs
Moving users from one server to the other one
Copying the code to a separate backup copy
items.explanation: New code may expect new tables or columns before it can run.

items.prompt: If the health check fails, where does traffic stay?
choices: It moves to the new release anyway
It is paused until someone fixes it
On the old release
items.explanation: A failed check means the switch never happens.

items.prompt: What does a release directory hold?
choices: Only the database tables and rows
One complete version of the app
Only the newest changed files
items.explanation: Each release folder is a full, self-contained version.

items.prompt: Why do migrations run before the health check rather than after the switch?
choices: Migrations are quick, so the order makes no real difference
The candidate needs its database changes before it can answer
Migrations run last would undo the pointer switch afterwards
The check cannot start until the old release has stopped
items.explanation: A candidate that lacks its database changes would fail the check for the wrong reason, and migrating after the switch would put users on a release not yet ready.
items.reference:
The fixed order
1. extract the new release
2. install dependencies
3. run migrations
4. health check on the candidate
5. atomic switch, then restart
Why: everything before the switch runs while the old release still serves users, so a failure there is invisible to them.
items.learnMore:
Why the order is fixed

Extract, install, migrate and check all work on a candidate nobody is routed to yet. The switch is the only step that changes what users reach, so it comes after the check has passed.

Common mistake

Putting the check after the switch. Users then reach the release before anyone knows whether it works.
items.reflection: Think of a task where you prepare everything before the one irreversible move, such as cooking before serving. What is your switch, and what is your check?

items.prompt: A team moves the health check to after 'restart service'. What changes?
choices: Users may be served a broken release before anyone notices
Nothing changes, since the check still runs once per deploy
The deploy gets faster and stays exactly as safe
The old release can no longer be kept live at all
items.explanation: After the switch real traffic is already on the new release. The check can still detect a failure but can no longer prevent exposure.

The check must run before extraction on the old release

The switch happens anyway and the check rolls back
Users stay on the old release, unaffected by it
The old release is stopped to free up resources
items.explanation: Install runs before the switch, so its failure leaves the old release serving as before.

items.prompt: What is a symlink?
choices: A pointer that names one folder
A full copy of that folder's files
A password that locks the folder
items.explanation: A symlink is a reference to a location, not a copy.

items.prompt: What does overwriting files in place risk?
choices: Deleting the database by accident
Using twice the disk space briefly
A window holding old and new files
items.explanation: Files are replaced one at a time, so for a moment the folder holds both versions.

items.prompt: How many in-between states can a pointer have?
choices: One
None
Many
items.explanation: It names either the old folder or the new one.

items.prompt: With a pointer switch each request gets:
choices: A fully old or a fully new version
A random mix of both old and new files
Half of each, split evenly between them
items.explanation: There is no way to read a mix when the pointer changes in one step.

items.prompt: Why is the word atomic used?
choices: The change is always very small in size
The change only ever touches a single file
The change happens as one indivisible step
items.explanation: Atomic means it either has happened or it has not.

items.prompt: In which approach do in-between states exist?
choices: The pointer switch
Overwriting in place
Both approaches to an equal degree
items.explanation: Replacing files one by one passes through mixed states.

items.prompt: Before the switch, where does the new version sit?
choices: In its own separate folder
Mixed into the live folder
Inside the database
items.explanation: Keeping it separate is what lets the switch be a single pointer change.

items.prompt: What does the switch change?
choices: The code inside the old folder
The size of the release folder
Which folder users are sent to
items.explanation: It repoints traffic. Nothing inside either folder is touched.

items.prompt: An in-place deploy overwrites three files one after another. How many mixed old-and-new states can a request land in?
choices: Three
One
Zero
Two
items.explanation: The states are new-old-old and new-new-old. All old and all new are not mixed, and a pointer switch would have none.
items.reference:
Overwrite or repoint
⚠️ in place: 3 files give 2 mixed states
↔️ a request can land in either one
✅ pointer: release-8 then release-9
✅ pointer: 0 mixed states
Why: a pointer names exactly one folder, so a request sees fully old or fully new code.
items.learnMore:
What atomic buys you

Overwriting files one at a time leaves a window where a request can read a mix of old and new files. A symlink switch changes one pointer, so there is no state between old and new.

Common mistake

Assuming atomic means correct. The switch rules out half-and-half states but says nothing about whether the new release is good.
items.reflection: Think of a change you made gradually that confused people half-way through, like rearranging a shared space. How could you have made it a single move?

items.prompt: Users see brief errors during deploys although checks pass. The pipeline copies new files into the live folder. What is the likely cause?
choices: The health check runs too often during every deploy
The live folder is too large to be read at once
Requests land between file copies and read a mix
Users have cached the old files in their browsers
items.explanation: Copying into the live folder creates the mixed-state window that a pointer switch avoids.

items.prompt: Which design makes the switch atomic?
choices: Extract over the live folder, then restart it very quickly
Extract into a new folder, then repoint one pointer
Copy files in a fixed order so older ones go first
Lock the live folder and copy the files much faster
items.explanation: Speed and ordering shrink the window but do not remove it. Only a single pointer change does.

items.prompt: Is an atomic switch alone enough to guarantee users never see a broken release?
choices: No, it prevents mixed states but not a bad release
Yes, atomic means the new release must be correct
Yes, since the old release is deleted at that instant
No, atomic switches only work on a single file
items.explanation: Atomicity is about the shape of the change. Correctness of the release is the health check's job.

items.prompt: What triggers the rollback branch in the pipeline?
choices: A person typing a command
A failed health check
A new commit being pushed
items.explanation: The branch is wired to the result of the check.

items.prompt: Who must remember the rollback in an automated pipeline?
choices: Nobody, it runs by itself after a failed check
The engineer who happens to be on call tonight
The person who originally wrote the code
items.explanation: The pipeline contains the rollback, so no memory is needed.

items.prompt: In a manual process, how is a bad deploy usually found?
choices: A script reports it automatically before launch
The team gets an alert from a monitoring tool
Someone notices symptoms, then investigates
items.explanation: Manual processes rely on someone seeing the problem.

items.prompt: Where must the check sit to keep users off a broken release?
choices: After the restart
Before the switch
After the first complaint
items.explanation: Only a check before the switch can prevent exposure.

items.prompt: After a failed check, which release stays live?
choices: The old release
The new release
Neither of them
items.explanation: The old release never stopped serving.

items.prompt: What can an idempotent pipeline do?
choices: Run exactly one time and then lock itself
Skip every step that failed on the last run
Be re-run after a failure and end correct
items.explanation: Idempotency makes retries safe.

items.prompt: Would a stricter checklist have prevented release 9?
choices: Yes, a stricter list cannot be skipped
Not reliably, it still depends on memory
Yes, as long as it is printed out and signed
items.explanation: A stricter page is still a page. It does not enforce anything.

items.prompt: How does recovery work in the manual column?
choices: Someone re-runs the old steps by hand
The rollback branch runs on its own
The health check repairs the broken files
items.explanation: Manual recovery needs a person to start and carry it out.

items.prompt: Why does a health check placed after restart behave like the manual column?
choices: It removes the need for any rollback at all
It detects and recovers, but cannot prevent exposure
It checks a different release than the pipeline built
It runs before the old release is stopped
items.explanation: After the switch users are already on the new release. The check only shortens the exposure.
items.reference:
Remembered versus automatic
manual: someone notices symptoms
manual: someone re-runs old steps
pipeline: check runs before the switch
pipeline: failure keeps the old release live
Why: when the pipeline's next step is the rollback, nobody has to remember it under pressure.
items.learnMore:
Automatic rollback

The health check runs before traffic switches, and a failure leads straight to keeping the old release live. Recovery is a branch of the pipeline, not a procedure someone must recall.

Common mistake

Having a written rollback page and calling it automated. If a person must remember to run it, it is still manual.
items.reflection: Think of a recovery plan you have only written down, such as a backup restore. What would make it run itself the moment it was needed?

items.prompt: A team has a health check, but rollback is a wiki page: 'run these commands if the check fails'. What is still missing?

A faster health check that reports a failure sooner
More steps in the checklist ahead of the check
A second reviewer who reads every check result
items.explanation: The detection is automated, but recovery still depends on a person recalling and carrying it out.

items.prompt: In a gated deploy, what runs right after preparation?
choices: The pointer switch
The restart
The health check
items.explanation: The check gates the switch.

items.prompt: When does the gate switch the pointer?
choices: Always, then check afterwards
Only if the check passes
Only after a person approves
items.explanation: The switch is conditional on a pass.

items.prompt: On a failed check, what does rollback mean here?
choices: Never switching; the old release stays
Switching back once users start to complain
Deleting the new release from disk forever
items.explanation: Users never left the old release.

items.prompt: Which steps count as preparation?
choices: Switch and restart the service
Only the final service restart
Extract, install and migrate
items.explanation: Preparation does not touch user traffic.

items.prompt: Which step is the only one that changes user traffic?
choices: Extracting the release files
Switching the pointer
Running migrations
items.explanation: Everything before it works on the candidate only.

items.prompt: What might implement the candidate check?
choices: A temporary port or preview route
A survey sent out to all users
A page kept on the team wiki
items.explanation: Any way of testing the new release before real traffic reaches it.

items.prompt: After a failed check, does the old release keep serving?
choices: No
Only after a restart
Yes
items.explanation: It never stopped serving.

items.prompt: Why does one failing call abandon a healthy but slow release?
choices: The gate retries three more times first
The gate treats one failure as final
The gate ignores the failure and goes on
items.explanation: One call cannot tell broken from still starting up.

items.prompt: The check passes. Which are the last two actions of the gated deploy?
choices: Restart the service, then switch the pointer
Run migrations, then switch the pointer
Switch the pointer, then run the check again
Switch the pointer, then restart the service
items.explanation: The switch is the final traffic-affecting step, and the restart follows it.
items.reference:
Prepare, check, then maybe switch
🧰 prepare: extract, install, migrate
🩺 check the candidate
✅ pass: switch pointer, restart
🛑 fail: keep the old release live
Why: the switch is the only step that touches user traffic, and it runs only after the check passes.
items.learnMore:
The gated deploy

Splitting preparation from the one step that changes traffic makes the rule explicit. A failed check means the pointer is never moved, which is why rollback here means never switching.

Common mistake

Retrying nothing. A single failing call is decisive, which can abandon a healthy release that was merely slow to start.

items.prompt: The check fails. Which list shows what the gate did, in order?
choices: Extract, install, migrate, switch, check, roll back
Extract, install, check, migrate, keep the old release live
Extract, install, migrate, check, keep the old release live
Extract, switch, install, migrate, check
items.explanation: Preparation comes first, then the check, then the old release stays because the switch is skipped.

choices: Switches anyway because the release is healthy
Keeps the old release and reports a failure
Retries until the release answers correctly
Waits for a person to decide what to do

items.prompt: Why might a health check retry?
choices: A healthy release may fail early checks
To make every deploy slower on purpose
To run extra tests on the database
items.explanation: Retrying gives a slow-starting release time to answer.

items.prompt: A release passes on its third check. With 1 attempt allowed, what happens?
choices: It passes
It waits 30 seconds then passes
It is rolled back by mistake
items.explanation: One attempt ends before the release is ready.

items.prompt: With 3 attempts allowed, the same release:
choices: Is rolled back by mistake
Passes on the third check
Passes on the first check
items.explanation: The third attempt is the first one it can pass.

items.prompt: With 5 attempts at 10 s apart, how long is the longest wait?
choices: 50 seconds
30 seconds
5 seconds
items.explanation: 5 attempts times 10 seconds is 50 seconds.

items.prompt: What is the cost of allowing too many attempts?
choices: Healthy deploys are rolled back by mistake
The old release is deleted too early
Broken releases linger as candidates longer
items.explanation: More attempts mean a longer wait before giving up.

items.prompt: What is the cost of allowing too few attempts?
choices: Broken deploys are never caught by the gate
Healthy but slow deploys get rolled back
The pointer ends up moving twice per deploy
items.explanation: A good release that needs warm-up is rejected early.

items.prompt: A truly broken release with 5 attempts:
choices: Fails every check and is caught after the fifth
Passes on the third check, then fails later on
Is never detected by any of the checks at all
items.explanation: A broken release does not start passing, so retries only add waiting.

items.prompt: Who decides the attempt count?
choices: A fixed industry rule that says use three
Whatever the wiki page says to use
Your own system's warm-up time and tolerance
items.explanation: The example numbers are a case, not a universal setting.

items.prompt: A healthy release needs 5 checks to pass, 10 seconds apart. What is the smallest setting that avoids a needless rollback?
choices: 4 attempts, 40 seconds of waiting
5 attempts, 50 seconds of waiting
3 attempts, 30 seconds of waiting
6 attempts, 60 seconds of waiting
items.explanation: It passes only on the fifth check, so at least 5 attempts are needed. 5 times 10 seconds is 50 seconds, and 6 would add waiting for nothing.
items.reference:
Healthy but slow passes on check 3
1 attempt: rolled back by mistake, 10 s
2 attempts: rolled back by mistake, 20 s
3 attempts: passes, 30 s
5 attempts: passes, 50 s
Why: too few attempts reject good deploys, while too many delay the verdict on broken ones.
items.learnMore:
The retry trade-off

A warming-up service may fail its first checks. Allowing a few attempts lets a healthy release pass, at the price of a longer wait before a truly broken release is dropped. The numbers here assume checks 10 seconds apart.

Common mistake

Treating one number as universal. The right attempt count depends on your own service's warm-up time and how long you can tolerate waiting.
items.reflection: Think of something that needs a warm-up before it works, like an engine or a sleepy colleague. How many tries before you decide it is broken?

items.explanation: 20 times 10 seconds is 200 seconds. A broken release fails every check, so every extra attempt only delays the verdict.

items.prompt: Implement `hasStep(steps, name)`. Return true if `name` appears in the list `steps`, otherwise false.
items.explanation: `includes` answers exactly the question asked and returns false for an empty list.

items.prompt: Implement `lastStep(steps)`. Return the final step name, or null for an empty list.
items.explanation: The empty list has no last element, so it needs its own answer rather than undefined.

items.prompt: Implement `stepNumber(steps, name)`. Return the 1-based position of `name`, or 0 if it is absent.
items.explanation: `indexOf` gives -1 when absent, so adding 1 turns it into 0 and shifts found positions to start from 1.

items.prompt: Implement `installStep(release)`. Return the string `install-deps:` followed by the release name.
items.explanation: A function that builds the step name from the release means every run produces it the same way.

items.prompt: Implement `stepsAfter(steps, name)`. Return the steps that come after `name`, or an empty list if `name` is absent.
items.explanation: An absent name gives index -1, which would wrongly slice from the start, so it is handled first.

items.prompt: Implement `withRollback(steps, healthy)`. Return a new list equal to `steps`, plus `rollback` at the end when `healthy` is false.
items.explanation: The rollback is part of the returned list, decided by the check result, not by someone remembering.

items.prompt: Implement `isComplete(required, actual)`. Return true if every step in `required` appears in `actual`.
items.explanation: `every` on an empty list is true, which is the right answer when nothing is required.

items.prompt: Implement `firstMissing(required, actual)`. Return the first required step not in `actual`, or null if none is missing.
items.explanation: Scanning in required order and returning at the first gap gives the earliest missing step.

items.prompt: Implement `missingSteps(required, actual)`. Return the steps in `required` that are not in `actual`, in the same order as `required`. Extra steps in `actual` are fine.
items.explanation: Filtering `required` keeps its order and drops everything that did run, so extras in `actual` never matter.
items.reference:
Small pure functions around a deploy
📋 required steps vs steps that ran
🔢 order matters: compare positions
🔁 retry: stop at the first pass
🚦 gate: switch only if healthy
Why: when you write the check yourself, you see exactly which cases a skipped step or a flaky check would slip through.
items.learnMore:
Writing the pipeline's checks

Each function here is a few lines: compare what ran with what was required, check order, retry until a pass, or choose between switching and keeping the old release. Writing them makes edge cases such as empty lists, extras and early stops concrete.

Common mistake

Forgetting the boundaries: an empty required list, extra steps that are allowed, and stopping at the first success rather than calling the check every time.
items.reflection: Think of a checklist in your own work. How would you write down, in one sentence, the rule that tells you a step was missed?

items.prompt: Implement `inOrder(required, actual)`. Return true if every step in `required` appears in `actual` in the same relative order. Extra steps in `actual` are allowed.
items.explanation: Each required step must be found after the previous one, so the search start only moves forward. A missing or out-of-order step makes the search fail.

items.prompt: Implement `retryHealthCheck(check, attempts)`. Call `check(n)` for n = 1, 2, 3 ... up to `attempts` times. Return the n of the first call that returns true, or 0 if none does. Stop calling as soon as one passes.

tests.expr: let calls = 0; const r = retryHealthCheck((n) => { calls += 1; return n >= 2; }, 5); expect(r).toBe(2); expect(calls).toBe(2)

items.explanation: Returning inside the loop stops at the first pass. Falling out of the loop means every attempt failed, or none was allowed, and gives 0.
